items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text:
TROPICAL TRIO OF 3 HURRICANES🌀🌀🌀the Eastern and Central Pacific remain extremely active with Hurricanes MARIE, LOWELL and KARINA all spinning at the same time!

🔴 MARIE is strengthening well southwest of Mexico and is forecast to continue generally west-northwest to northwest over the open Eastern Pacific. The storm is expected to stay well away from Mexico and the continental U.S., but moisture associated with Marie could eventually get pulled north toward parts of California and the Southwest this weekend into early next week. Again, direct impacts are not expected.

🔴 LOWELL is the monster of the three, briefly reaching Category 5 strength, about 400 miles south of Hilo. Lowell is moving west and is currently forecast to remain south of Hawaii, with no tropical watches or warnings in effect at this time. However, this hurricane needs to be monitored closely as some guidance suggest a faster northward turn, bringing impacts to Hawaii but the current forecast from the NHC does not indicate a direct impact.

🔴 KARINA remains a powerful Category 4 hurricane with 140 mph winds far east of Hawaii. It is moving west-northwest and is forecast to gradually weaken over the next several days. The NHC currently lists no direct land impacts from Karina, and there are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.

So far, none of the three hurricanes is forecast to make landfall in Hawaii, Mexico or the continental U.S., but Lowell will bring increasing surf to Hawaii and needs to be monitored closely, and Marie's moisture could eventually influence weather across portions of the Southwest and California🌊🌧️

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text:
SOCAL & SW FLASH FLOOD RISK THIS WEEKEND ⚠️tropical moisture associated with Hurricane Marie will spread across Southern California and the Southwest this weekend, increasing shower and thunderstorm chances! The WPC has included parts of the region in an isolated flash-flood risk. Across Southern California, moisture will increase substantially from Saturday into Sunday. Showers and isolated thunderstorms are possible across Los Angeles, Ventura, Orange, San Diego, Riverside and San Bernardino counties. Slow-moving or repeated storms could produce locally heavy rain and flash flooding, especially across the mountains, deserts, burn scars and normally dry washes. Light to moderate rain remains the most likely outcome around Los Angeles and Ventura, but isolated heavier thunderstorms cannot be ruled out. 

The threat will also extend into southeastern California and southern Nevada, where storms could become fairly widespread Saturday and increase Sunday. Heavy rainfall and storms repeatedly crossing the same locations may cause flash flooding. Around Phoenix and Tucson, and across south-central and western Arizona, localized heavy rain and isolated flash flooding will also be possible. 

Extensive cloud cover may limit the overall intensity of storms, but considerable uncertainty remains on instability as well as the track of Marie, which will have significant impacts on the forecast🌧️⛈️

WIND AND LAKE WIND ADVISORIES ACROSS NORTHERN CALIFORNIA, THE SIERRA AND WESTERN NEVADA⚠️a strong early-season storm is producing gusty winds across parts of Northern California, the Sierra and western Nevada. Wind Advisories remain in effect through 8PM today for Del Norte and Humboldt counties, where south winds of 20-30 mph could gust between 45 and 50 mph. The strongest gusts are expected along exposed ridges and coastal headlands. Drivers, especially those in high-profile vehicles, should use extra caution.

Farther east, Lake Wind Advisories remain in effect through 11PM Thursday for Lake Tahoe, Pyramid Lake and numerous other lakes and reservoirs across northeastern California, the eastern Sierra and western Nevada. Southwest winds of 15-25 mph could gust to 30 mph, with gusts up to 35 mph at Pyramid Lake. Waves of 1-3 feet are possible on Lake Tahoe and Pyramid Lake. In Mono County, southwest winds of 10–20 mph with gusts up to 30 mph will affect Topaz Lake, Bridgeport Reservoir, Mono Lake and Crowley Lake. Strong winds and rough waves will create hazardous conditions for small boats. Check lake conditions before heading out, remain prepared for winds and waves to increase suddenly, and consider postponing boating activities until conditions improve🌊⚠️

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
As of 5 pm on September 2, 2026 now ranks 5th on the list of latest dates for the Atlantic season’s first hurricane.

And we may not be done climbing that list.

Right now, neither the physics-based models nor the AI models show much of a signal for hurricane development over the next 10 days. If that holds, we could eventually break the record for the latest first hurricane on record.

That begs the question: Has the Atlantic ever gone an entire season without a hurricane?

Technically, yes. The 1907 and 1914 seasons have no hurricanes in the historical record. But both occurred long before the weather satellite era began in 1966. Back then, if a hurricane formed far out over the open Atlantic and never encountered a ship or land, there was a good chance no one ever knew it existed.

So while the record books say there were no hurricanes in those two seasons, it’s certainly possible there were storms spinning harmlessly over the middle of the Atlantic that simply went undetected.

I'd be fine with a big fat zero on the board for 2026!

items.text:
A new study published last month highlights the Gulf Stream's variability.

The study looked at satellite data over a 31-year period from 1993 to 2024 and found the Gulf Stream intensified significantly from 2014 to 2023. This was preceded by a period of Gulf Stream weakening from 2005-2014. 

The study shows the Gulf Stream is not constant and goes through periods of higher & lower activity. The study was an observational one & did not look at why these changes were happening, but the variation is part of a larger ocean current system known as the "subtropical gyre." 

The Gulf Stream transports heat from the southern latitudes to the North Atlantic & the higher latitudes, increasing heat release to the atmosphere & warming the upper ocean.  

They found that when weaker, the portion of the Gulf Stream in the North Atlantic flows farther south, leading to colder & drier winters across Europe. A stronger Gulf Stream flows farther north, leading to wetter & warmer winters in Europe, especially western Europe.    

The study shows how complicated & dynamic Earth's ocean current system is, making it difficult to describe & generalize in simple rules or statements. 

Very interesting!   

Study info: https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/satellite-data-reveals-gulf-stream-intensification/

AROUND THIS TIME 18 YEARS AGO, #Gustav made landfall along the #Louisiana coast near Cocodrie as a Category 2 hurricane.

It came just three years after #Katrina, and Gulf Coast anxiety couldn't have been any higher... everyone was on edge.

While Gustav was still in the Caribbean as a Category 4, New Orleans mayor Ray Nagin called it "the storm of the century."

Thankfully, it wasn't the storm of the century, but it did still pack a major punch.

First and foremost, it was the first massive evacuation of SE Louisiana since Katrina — about 2 million people left the Louisiana coast ahead of landfall.

Storm surge of 10-14 ft hit parts of Louisiana's coast. It caused an estimated $6-7 billion in damage in the United States.

While I was working at the TV station in Baton Rouge from 2011-2014, I spoke to many locals who said Gustav was the worst storm they had ever been through there.

It was yet another example that the "category" of a storm doesn't always tell the whole story. Even though Gustav was "only" a 110 mph Category 2 at landfall in Louisiana, the impacts proved how dangerous lower-category hurricanes can still be.

It is worth noting, there is sufficient helicity (twisting) to the atmosphere to warrant at least some risk for tornadoes. It's not impossible a few of these could be strong. But the fact remains the risk for tornadoes is much greater later today than any other typical day in this part of the world. Best to be prepared, just in case.

EL NIÑO GIVETH, AND EL NIÑO TAKETH AWAY

One of the classic hallmarks of El Niño is a tale of two oceans...a very busy tropical Pacific and a relatively quiet Atlantic. Extremely warm water and light wind shear in the Pacific are helping fuel tropical activity, while El Niño has brought relentless wind shear and sinking air to the Atlantic, making it very difficult for tropical storms and hurricanes to develop and strengthen.

Right now, the Pacific is loaded. There are two major hurricanes and a tropical storm nearing hurricane strength. Hurricane Lowell is on the verge of Category 5 intensity with 155 mph winds, while Hurricane Karina is a Category 4 with 145 mph winds. Tropical Storm Marie is also forecast to become a hurricane soon. None of these systems are a threat to Hawaii. 

Meanwhile, over in the Atlantic...crickets. Not a single system is expected to develop over the next seven days.

Quite the tale of two oceans!

Long before Mom passed away, Cindy and I made spending time with our parents a priority. We’re blessed to have both of our families here in Myrtle Beach, and we’ve always known how precious that time is. With Mom confined to a wheelchair, she especially loved when Dad or we would take her out for breakfast, lunch or dinner. Looking back, I’m so grateful for those seemingly ordinary moments because today they mean everything.

Tuesday morning, Cindy and I had breakfast with Dad at Zeytin. Nothing fancy, no special occasion, just breakfast together. But these are exactly the moments we cherish even more now. Since Mom passed, we’ve been spending more time with Dad, Momma Linda and Papa Wade. Not out of sympathy or obligation, but because losing Mom reinforced something we already knew: you never get time back, and you never know how much of it you have with the people you love.

That realization has really affected me personally. I find myself thinking about my mortality far more than I used to. I’ll turn 60 in December, and sometimes I struggle with just how quickly life seems to be passing. I’ve spent years telling people to take life one day at a time, and now I’m realizing just how hard it can be to take my own advice.

So when those thoughts creep in, I turn to Cindy and we lean on our faith. Jesus says in Matthew 6:34, “Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.” And Psalm 90:12 says, “Teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” Maybe numbering our days isn’t about worrying how many we have left, but appreciating the one we have today.

I can’t control how much time I have, and worrying about it certainly won’t give me any more. What I can do is make the most of the time God gives me...to love Cindy, cherish Dad, Momma Linda and Papa Wade, spend time with the people who matter most, and keep making memories.

I’m trying to leave tomorrow with God and be thankful for today. I know that’s what I need to do. But knowing it and actually doing it are two very different things.

MARIE & SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA: SEVERAL LABOR DAY WEEKEND OUTCOMES REMAIN POSSIBLE🌀🌧️⛈️Tropical Storm Marie has formed in the Eastern Pacific and is expected to strengthen into a Hurricane. While a direct tropical storm or hurricane impact on Southern California remains very unlikely - almost 0, Marie could still have noticeable impacts on the region this Labor Day weekend and into early next week. The key is Marie’s exact track and its interaction with an upper-level low lingering near the Pacific Northwest. The most likely scenario keeps Marie well offshore while the larger weather pattern pulls some of its tropical moisture northeastward into Southern California and eventually the Great Basin.

At this point, there is roughly a 55-65% chance of widespread light rainfall across parts of Southern California Sunday through Monday night, generally around 0.2-0.60 inches looks most probable. However, there is also about a 15-20% chance of a wetter and stormier outcome involving heavier rainfall and thunderstorms. If thunderstorms develop within the tropical moisture plume, locally heavier rainfall and flooding concerns could emerge.

There is another completely different outcome worth watching - the dry side. If the pattern develops differently, and Marie remains well offshore, gusty offshore, easterly winds could develop ahead of the moisture that could increase fire-weather concerns in parts of Southern California before any rainfall arrives. This only has about a 10-15% chance of happening.

So, long story short, there is still a fairly wide array of possibilities, but the most probable is for light to moderate rain occurring across parts of Southern California this weekend into early next week. The important point is that Marie does not have to make landfall in California to influence the weather. Even hundreds of miles offshore, its moisture can be pulled northward into the region. 

Small changes in Marie’s track could make a significant difference in how much moisture ultimately reaches Southern California so expect the forecast to continue changing as Marie strengthens and its track becomes better established over the next few days🌀🌧️⛈️

CENTER INTERCEPT! I normally don’t go after tropical storms or low end hurricanes so this was a first of a kind outing for me today. 

Edouards tiny size and only 4 mile wide eye (at times) made it a challenge. They eye got flung around insure what looked like a bigger eye, making positioning for the landfall tricky, but pulled it off.

What really surprised me about this one was the intensity of western eyewall. In most tropical systems it’s usually the right front quadrant that gets the most intense winds, but not this one. It seemed to strengthen after making landfall continuing to produce gusts as high as 90mph 2 hours after the fact.

All in all a useful day out in the field. It’s really a good thing the storm had a short time over water, that final hour or so before landfall it really slipped a switch and began cranking. A unique storm, and one that’s good to learn from. 

Parts of Texas and Louisiana are a little messy and without power, but thankfully nothing worse! Thanks to everyone who shared important weather info to their family friends and neighbors!

EL NINO HAS THE ATLANTIC IN A HEADLOCK

September 1st normally means we’re heading straight into the heart of hurricane season, when the Atlantic is typically at its busiest.

Instead…crickets.

A historic El Niño continues to make conditions increasingly hostile for tropical development across the Atlantic. In simple terms, El Niño has basically hung a “NO VACANCY” sign over the tropics.

And the quiet looks like it may stick around. Nothing is expected to develop over the next 7 days, and the longer-range guidance doesn’t show much reason for concern through the next 10-14 days either.

That’s especially impressive considering we’re closing in on the September 10th climatological peak of hurricane season.

Of course, we’re not letting our guard down. Hurricane season runs through November 30th, and it only takes one storm to make it a devastating season.

For now, though, we’ll gladly take boring.

BUSY PACIFIC WITH 3 HURRICANES, INCLUDING 2 MAJOR HURRICANES THIS WEEK🌀🌀🌀the Eastern and Central Pacific are extremely active this week, with three eventual hurricanes in the picture! Lowell, Karina and soon-to-be Hurricane Marie.

Forecast models generally show Lowell eventually turning north after passing west of the Islands, so Hawaii will continue to closely monitor its progress

This is the system garnering all of the interest. A direct strike from Marie on Southern California remains VERY UNLIKELY, but that does not mean the storm will have zero impacts. Tropical moisture associated with Marie will be pulled into California and the Southwest this weekend into early next week, increasing the potential for showers and thunderstorms, and possibly some flooding. Large swells from Marie are also expected to reach Southern California this weekend, bringing an increased risk of dangerous surf and rip currents

❄️ Pluto may still have liquid moving across its surface.

A new analysis of NASA’s New Horizons images has found evidence that liquid nitrogen may be rising through cracks in Sputnik Planitia, the giant heart-shaped glacier on Pluto.

This is not liquid water.

Sputnik Planitia is made largely of frozen nitrogen, and Pluto is so cold that nitrogen behaves there in ways water does on Earth.

The clue comes from dark, narrow and diffuse features along the northern edge of the glacier.

They resemble places on Earth’s ice sheets where liquid briefly wets the surface and darkens the snow or ice.

But on Pluto, nitrogen rain is physically impossible under its current atmospheric and thermal conditions.

That leaves a stranger possibility.

Computer models suggest that nitrogen ice at the base of Pluto’s kilometer-deep glacier could melt under stress, forming liquid nitrogen.

That liquid could then rise through small conduits, reach the surface and remain liquid long enough to flow downhill before freezing again.

The surface of Sputnik Planitia is probably less than a million years old, so these features may be geologically recent.

Pluto was supposed to be a frozen dead world.

Instead, it may still be leaking liquid from beneath its icy heart.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Stern et al., “Evidence for Possible N₂ Basal Flow beneath Pluto’s Northern Sputnik Planitia”, The Planetary Science Journal (2026)

EARY-SEASON WINDS FOR PNW🌬️⚠️🌲a strong early-season storm will bring widespread gusty winds to the Pacific Northwest on Wednesday, with some areas potentially seeing enough wind for downed tree limbs and power outages. One concern is that trees across much of the region are still fully leafed out, allowing them to catch more wind than they would during a typical fall or winter storm. After a long, dry summer, stressed trees and branches may also be more vulnerable, so expect scattered downed limbs and localized power outages, especially along the Washington and Oregon coasts. Secure loose outdoor objects and be prepared for brief power disruptions. Winds peak during the day Wednesday before gradually easing Wednesday night into Thursday.

Across Western Washington, gusts of 35-40 mph are expected along the coast, San Juan Islands and Whidbey Island, where a Wind Advisory is in effect. Western Whatcom and Skagit counties and the Port Townsend area could also see stronger gusts. Elsewhere across western Washington, gusts of 20-35 mph are expected.

Down into western Oregon, winds will become considerably stronger near the coast, with gusts along beaches and headlands potentially reaching 55-60 mph. Inland areas could gust around 30 mph, while the Columbia River Gorge and Hood River Valley could approach 40 mph.

Farther inland, the Inland Northwest will see south to southwest winds will gust 20-40 mph Wednesday, with some of the strongest winds across central Washington and the Columbia Basin. Blowing dust could reduce visibility in the drier areas🌬️⚠️🌲

items.author: ryanhallyall
items.text: If you want to catch something in the sky tonight, plan on being outside before dawn. Saturn is riding high in the southern sky and Mars is glowing lower over in the east, and neither one needs a telescope, just find an open view and look up. A 74 percent gibbous moon rises around 10:07 PM Central and will wash out a lot of the fainter stars, but Saturn and Mars are plenty bright to hold their own against that glow. Tonight's driest air and lowest cloud cover stretch from the southern Plains through the lower Ohio Valley and into the Southeast, with Columbus, Charlotte, Indianapolis and San Antonio all shaping up nicely. A few spots to skip if you can: the Bay Area is dealing with an incoming front and low clouds, coastal Southern California has gusty winds and marine fog, and parts of the northern Great Lakes and coastal Texas have their own storm chances tonight. As for the northern lights, tonight is about as quiet as it gets, Kp is only running around 2, so any glow stays confined to the far northern tier and would really only show up on a camera, not something to expect from the Lower 48.

The night sky of September is magical 💫👇🏻

♀️ Sep 1: Venus Kisses Spica
Brilliant Venus slides right past Spica, the blue-white heart of Virgo. The dazzling planet and the star form a striking close pair in the fading evening twilight.
📍 Visibility: Low in the west-southwest, about 45 minutes after sunset. Binoculars help; far better placed from the Southern Hemisphere, where the evening sky stands steeper.

🌠 Sep 1–2: Aurigid Meteor Shower
A minor but intriguing shower peaks in the small hours, shed by comet Kiess on its ~2,000-year orbit. The Aurigids are sparse but famous for the occasional brilliant fireball.
📍 Visibility: Best from the Northern Hemisphere in the hours before dawn; the radiant sits in Auriga, rising in the northeast. A bright waning gibbous Moon washes out all but the brightest this year (~6/hour at best).

🌙 Sep 6–7: Moon Meets Mars
The waning crescent Moon glides up to reddish Mars in Gemini, close to the bright twin stars Castor and Pollux — a delicate pre-dawn grouping.
📍 Visibility: Eastern sky before sunrise, both hemispheres. Mars is faint this month, so let the crescent Moon guide your eye to it.

🌒 Sep 14: Moon Occults Venus
The thin crescent Moon passes directly in front of Venus, briefly hiding the brightest planet behind its edge — a rare occultation.
📍 Visibility: The true occultation is visible from parts of Asia (including Malaysia) and, in daylight, Europe; elsewhere it's a close Moon–Venus pairing low in the west after sunset. A tough catch, with Venus sitting low in bright twilight.

🍂 Sep 23: Autumn Equinox
Day and night fall into near-perfect balance as the Sun crosses the celestial equator. Autumn begins in the Northern Hemisphere; spring stirs in the Southern.
📍 Visibility: Worldwide. The equinox arrives at 00:05 UTC on Sep 23 (the evening of the 22nd in the Americas).

🌕 Sep 26: Harvest Moon
The full Moon closest to the equinox rises golden on the horizon, with ringed Saturn glowing close by. For several nights running it climbs just after sunset — the hallmark of the Harvest Moon.
📍 Visibility: Worldwide. Rises around sunset; look east as darkness falls, with Saturn (near opposition) as a bonus alongside.

This photo is a microcosm of what our lives looked like over the last few years before Mom passed.

As many of you know, her health was not great so she spent a lot of time in and out of hospitals, rehab facilities and doctors’ offices. One of her longer stays away from home was at Brightwater, where she went for rehab after surgery to repair a broken tibia.

We visited her every single day for several months. There were times when it was mentally and physically exhausting, but Mom thrived when we were there. She was always so happy to see us, and no matter how tired we might have been, seeing her smile had a way of reinvigorating us.

Looking back now, I realize just how precious those days were.

There were so many great conversations, so much laughter and a lot of reminiscing about when we were kids, and how Mom somehow managed to put up with all four of us. At the time, they were simply visits. Today, they’re memories I wouldn’t trade for anything.

This photo gives a whole new meaning to simply sitting on the porch and relaxing. Whenever we could, we’d get Mom out of her room and into the fresh air. Nothing fancy. Just sitting together, talking and enjoying each other’s company.

I guess all of this is to say that some of life’s most meaningful moments don’t happen in the places or circumstances we would choose. Even in places that are far from ideal or normal, wonderful and lasting memories can be made.

Sometimes you don’t realize just how special those ordinary moments are until you’d give anything to have one more of them.

Current winds are around 40 mph but the NHC believes the system may have 60-70 mph winds by the time it reaches the southeast Texas coast midday today. Landfall is most likely near Beaumont. 

The wind or surge will not be major issues with this storm. Only a few isolated spots will actually see strong winds. 

The biggest issues with systems like this is rain. Rainfall totals generally of 3-6" are likely with some spots getting 4-8"+ in the heaviest rain bands. 

My main concern is that much of the heaviest rain will fall overnight in parts of east & southeast Texas. Overnight flooding is a serious concern as those who are traveling overnight will have a difficult time spotting flooded roadways. If you can, alter your plans to travel during the daylight hours as much as possible to make the trip a bit easier.  

The remnants of Edouard will weaken quickly as they drift NW on Wednesday, with most of the storm gone by Thursday, falling apart somewhere near Waco, well south of Dallas/Ft. Worth.

🍁HELLO, FALL!🍁

Well, meteorological fall, that is! It officially begins today. Astronomical fall, on the other hand, won’t kick in until September 22nd. So why the difference?

Astronomical seasons are tied to Earth’s position relative to the sun, while meteorological seasons follow the annual temperature cycle. In weather terms, winter is the three coldest months (Dec–Feb), summer the three hottest (Jun–Aug), with spring (Mar–May) and fall (Sep–Nov) bridging the gap.

And honestly? This is my favorite time of year. After sweating through a hot, sticky summer, I am more than ready for some crisp, dry, refreshing air. 
🍁🍂🍁🍂🍁
